## Do debt and growth dance together? A DSGE model of a small

## open economy with sovereign debt

Zixi Liu

July 2015

Draft version

## Abstract

Regarding the financial crisis since 2008, one heated debate lies in the relationships between

public debt and economic growth. The present paper develops a theoretical model in a small

open economy with sovereign risk based on Galí and Monacelli (2005, 2008). A country-

specific sovereign risk parameter is inserted into the sovereign interest rate equation to

analyze its influence to the links between debt and growth. This paper shows that there is no

single threshold and additionally, the relationship between debt and growth is country-specific

and it varies depending on the degree of sovereign risk. Three scenarios are considered

conditional on one set of randomly drawn simulated exogenous shocks. In a country with a

high sovereign risk, there is a negative relationship between debt and growth whereby debt-

GDP ratio is above 90%. With an extremely high sovereign risk, the relationship turns out to

be rather negative and the turning point is quite low. In some countries that sovereign risk is

not that high, fiscal stimulus could be effective to improve the economic growth. Moreover,

the relationships between debt and growth under the three scenarios are all hump-shaped.

JEL Classification Numbers: E62, F41, H30, H60

Keywords: growth, sovereign debt, DSGE, fiscal policy

## 1. Introduction

Under the debt crisis, countries in EMU are facing essential fiscal challenges. In the wake of

deteriorating public finances, countries, like Greece, Spain, Portugal, are implementing fiscal

austerity to restore fiscal sustainability. For example, Greece conducts fiscal austerity with a

change in the government deficit in percentage of GDP from -9.9% in 2008 to -8.6% in 2012,

as the debt-GDP ratio increases from 109.3% in 2008 to 174.9 % in 2013. Meanwhile, the real

GDP is declining since 2008 and by the end of 2013, the percentage change of real GDP

growth rate on previous year is still a negative number, -3.9%2. France is willing to implement

fiscal stimulus instead of fiscal austerity in late 2014 to boom the economy. On the other hand,

as Austria chooses a moderate fiscal austerity with the government deficit in percentage of

GDP varying from -5.3% in 2009 to -1.5% in 2013 and the debt to GDP ratio increasing to

81.2% in 2013, the real GDP is increasing slightly. As to Germany, a slowly fiscal adjustment

brings the government deficit in percentage of GDP a slight change from -3.0% to 0.1%,

when the debt to GDP ratio moves to 76.9% in 2013 and the real GDP goes up gradually. 3

In order to mitigate high debt, normally, government would like to choose fiscal austerity,

including government spending cuts and tax increases. In a country with a high level of public

debt, fiscal austerity would be perceived to be permanent and the soundness of public

finances would strengthen confidence among all economic participants. In this situation,

sovereign risk premium and inflation expectations become lower, resulting in a reduction in

interest rate. This may lead to an increase in the market value of wealth held by the private

sector and raise the aggregate demand through wealth effect. Besides, since households may

treat debt reduction as a signal of lower future tax burden and then a rise in permanent income,

higher aggregate demand could also be triggered. Therefore, the difference among above

examples may be associated with the country-specific debt burden, which is always measured

as debt-GDP ratio. Therefore, it seems interesting and worthy to investigate the relationship

between debt and economic growth at the country level.

A growing amount of empirical papers studies the relationship between debt and growth. Two

camps stand on the ground. One argues that high debt levels are associated with particularly

negative effects on economic growth. It requires fiscal austerity to cut debt levels to stimulate

the economy during financial crisis. On the other hand, an opposing perspective claims that

the priority should be fiscal stimulus rather than debt reduction since they believe that the

weak growth is the cause of rather high debt levels.

Some authors find evidence for the nonlinearity between debt and growth (See Kumar and

Woo (2010), Cecchetti et al (2012), Baum et al (2012), Checherita-westphal et al (2012b),

E gert (2012).). The widespread perspective is that the relationship between debt and growth

shows an inverse U-shape. Checherita-westphal et al (2012b) find an inverted U-shaped

relationship between public debt and growth for 12 euro area countries. In contrast, E gert

(2012) finds a U-shaped curve with a sample of 20 advanced economies over the period 1946-

2009. Additionally, threshold effect is especially the vital component of this popular academic

and political debate. An influential series of papers written by Reinhart and Rogoff (2010,

2012) find that economic growth is dramatically worse whereby debt-GDP ratio is above 90

percent, but there is no association between debt and growth when public debt is below 90

percent of GDP. While, due to a coding error, Reinhart and Rogoff (2010) is challenged by

Herdon et al (2013) saying that there seems no threshold effect exist. Cecchetti et al (2012)

find that beyond 96 percent, public debt becomes a drag on growth. Only considering Euro

Area, Baum et al (2012) find that debt has a non-linear effect on growth and there exists a

lower growth when it exceeds 95 percent. With the data from 13 OECD countries, E gert

(2012) states that there is a strong negative nonlinear relationship between debt and growth

and the threshold is between 20% and 60%. Pescatori et al (2014) uses an approach similar to

Reinhart and Rogoff (2010) when they discuss the short-run association between debt and

growth. They find that there is a substantial growth reduction when the debt-GDP ratio is

quite high and that there is no evidence of a particular debt threshold but debt trajectory is

likely to have an influence on future economic growth.

As to theoretical literatures, Checherita-Westphal et al (2012a) derive a hump-shaped relation

between debt and growth from a simple endogenous growth model assuming that government

implements the so-called golden-rule over the cycle, that is, deficits are equal to public

investment at each point of time. However, Greiner (2012) suspects that the results are driven

by their specific assumption and there is no well-specified model that can generate an inverted

U-shaped relationship between debt and growth. Teles et al (2013) develop an endogenously

growth model demonstrating the negative impact of the level of debt-GDP ratio on the

economic growth. Bi (2012) produces a non-linear relationship between the government debt


<!-- Page 6 -->


4

level and sovereign risk interest rate. Corsetti et al (2013) suggest under an extremely high

sovereign risk, fiscal retrenchment could stimulate the economy.

In the current studies of the relationship between debt and growth, usually, a general

relationship between debt and growth is discussed. However, a general relationship between

debt and growth may not work in a particular country. The relationship should be country-

specific. Therefore, in order to incorporate it into my research, I define a parameter measuring

country-specific sovereign risk to find a country-specific relationship between debt and

growth from a theoretical view.

I develop a DSGE model in a small open economy based on Galí and Monacelli (2005, 2008).

Assume that the model contains a home country and the rest of world. The domestic country

is so small such that any shock in its economy has no influence on the foreign economy. The

key difference lies in the fact that I adopt an incomplete asset market instead of a complete

securities market. Additionally, I introduce law of one price gap following Monacelli (2005).

Government issues one-period non-state-contingent bond in both domestic and international

financial markets and collects distortionary tax revenues to finance government spending. A

positive and non-linear relationship between debt-GDP ratio and the sovereign government

bond interest rate are introduced. This correlation is widely studied in empirical and

theoretical studies. (See Baldacci and Kumar (2010), Ardagna et al (2007), Eggertsson and

Woodford (2003)). Heavier government indebtedness leads to higher sovereign interest rate. I

also define a parameter measuring country-specific sovereign risk since I want to find a

country-specific relationship between debt and growth. A general relationship between debt

and growth may not work in a particular country. The relationship should depend on the

country-specific parameter. Although “country-specific sovereign risk” has already been

studied in earlier theoretical literatures, it is first used to analyze the relationship between debt

and growth in a DSGE model. This sovereign risk parameter tells an additional story between

debt-GDP ratio and sovereign interest rate. It demonstrates that sovereign interest rate is not

just related to debt-GDP ratio, but country-specific sovereign risk also plays a key role.

An incomplete market 4 is considered in my model which is quite different from other

literatures dealing with small open economy issues. Most literatures prefer to establish and

solve the model under a complete market assumption for simplicity. However, completeness

4 Details on this issue are discussed in section 2.12.


<!-- Page 7 -->


5

is rather unrealistic especially for some highly-indebted country, like Greece, Spain, and

Portugal. First, households in a high indebted country do not have the access to insure

themselves against the uncertainty of future economic shocks. Second, a risk premium to hold

foreign assets presents the fact that a complete set of assets is missing. This modification is

quite interesting and valuable for the economic analysis under the financial crisis.

Under complete asset markets assumption, domestic consumption is associated with world

consumption and terms of trade at the international level (See Galí and Monacelli (2005)). In

comparison, if markets are incomplete and there is a debt-elastic interest rate, domestic

consumption is tightly related to debt-GDP ratio since a higher debt-GDP ratio will cause a

lower aggregate demand and there would come an economic downturn afterwards.

The paper shows that there is no single threshold and additionally, the relationship between

debt and growth is country-specific and it varies depending on the degree of sovereign risk.

Two contributions arise. One is that this paper is the first to investigate the relationship

between debt and growth within a DSGE framework. The second is that the model can

illustrate some typical empirical results, which means that the model makes sense and could

be used in future research to investigate relative issues in an indebted small open economy.

In the present paper, based on the simulations, I try to investigate the relationship between

debt and growth from a theoretical view. The paper proceeds as follows. Next section clarifies

the detailed theoretical model. Section 3 lists the essential results. Section 4 offers some

conclusions.

### 2.12 Incomplete asset markets and sovereign interest rate

Most literatures take complete asset markets as an essential assumption in establishing open

economy models. It plays a key role in linking the domestic consumption with world

consumption and the terms of trade (See Galí and Monacelli (2005)). However, this

assumption is unrealistic considering current situations in highly indebted countries.

Households in these rather risky countries are facing the considerable uncertainty of the future

economic situation and they do not have any ability to insure themselves against the future

shocks. The inability to receive a return in every contingency through constructing a portfolio

in advance means that financial markets are incomplete. Moreover, if households participate

the international financial markets, a risk premium they have to pay reflects the fact that a

complete set of assets is missing and not everybody in the asset markets can exchange every

good with each other directly or indirectly without transaction costs.

A sovereign risk premium might be presented on domestic government bonds to reflect the

underlying default risk if the country has a high level of sovereign debt. Debt-GDP ratio plays

an essential role in determining sovereign interest rate. A reduction in debt-GDP ratio causes a

decrease in sovereign interest rate and an increase both in aggregate consumption and

investment, which could lead to an economic boom. Additionally, I introduce a country-

specific sovereign risk parameter to measure the relative change in risk premium due to the

variation in net level of domestic bonds. The more risky a country is, the higher the risk

premium is. According to García-Cicco et al (2010), Bi (2011), Cosetti et al (2010), the

positive relationship between sovereign interest rate and debt-GDP ratio (𝑥𝑡

### 2.21 Price setting and inflation dynamics

It is assumed that firms set prices in a staggered way according to Calvo (1983). Each period,

### 2.4 Macroeconomic stabilization policy in a small open economy with a fixed exchange

rate

In a small open economy with a fixed exchange rate, monetary policy cannot be conducted

through a Taylor rule. The currency peg means that the relative price level between domestic

and foreign country is pinned down in the long run and this is sufficient to close the model

and ensure long-run stability.9 However, as for stabilizing the economy in the medium and

short run, fiscal policy should be implemented.

The inefficiencies of a New-Keynesian DSGE model are introduced through monopolistic

competition and nominal rigidities. These price distortions may be relieved with either

monetary or fiscal policy. Generally, Taylor rule is perceived as an approximately reasonable

optimal monetary policy rule aiming at stabilizing the inflation and output gap to minimize

the welfare loss through adjusting the short-term interest rate. Nevertheless, in a small open

economy with a fixed exchange rate, a discretionary fiscal policy should be conducted instead

of Taylor rule to stabilize the economy. I include an artificial Taylor rule, the only role of

which is to provide a signal about the interest rate smoothing that responds to economic

fluctuations gradually. 10

consumption and government spending, and therefore, the steady-state consumption to GDP

### 3.11 Simulations and methodology

Simulation can provide a set of time series and the structure of the model economy. I adopt a

negative government spending shock to capture the idea of fiscal austerity. I simulate 500

periods16 from the model. A time period stands for one quarter.

the simulations of the two variables. It is possible that a different relationship between debt

The four exogenous shocks are independent of each other. Every shock is i.i.d distributed

following a normal distribution with zero mean and a respective standard deviation. Each

simulated exogenous variable is randomly drawn from its distribution. Therefore, all

randomly drawn simulated exogenous shocks are independent of each other. Besides, since all

the simulated exogenous variables are independent of each other, the simulated endogenous

variables are independent of each other. Therefore, I choose a simple OLS to establish the

relationship between the two variables.

Non-linearities between debt and growth have been widely approved. Empirical papers

always choose a quadratic specification to address the issue (See Checherita-westphal et al

(2012b), E gert (2012)). Moreover, Checherita-westphal et al (2012b) propose that the hump-

shaped relationship between debt and growth is robust to a more general polynomial function.

Therefore, I impose a quadratic functional form.

Additionally, since all the simulations refer to the percentage deviation of the steady state, in

order to analyze the relationship between debt and growth, the original simulations have to be

adjusted. First, adding the value of the steady state, 60%, to the simulated debt-GDP ratio, the

adjusted simulated debt-GDP ratio becomes an “actual” debt-GDP ratio. Second, economic

growth rate is achieved by subtracting the simulated output in the previous period from the

one in the current period. Besides, I exclude some extreme values with a negative or larger

than 210% debt-GDP ratio that are not common in the realistic world.

### 3.12 The non-linear relationship between debt and growth: three scenarios

There is no simple relationship and no single threshold (See IMF (2012), Pescatori et al

(2014)). This heterogeneity in both the non-linear relationship and the threshold effect may


<!-- Page 20 -->


18

result from miscellaneous samples and diverse country-specific patterns. (See Checherita-

westphal et al (2012b), E gert (2012), Reinhart and Rogoff (2010), Cecchetti et al (2012),

Baum et al (2012)).

Following Bi (2011), I denote γ = 0.1 as benchmark case and γ = 0.2 as high sovereign risk

case.17 Moreover, I consider a quite extreme case where γ = 0.9. 18

In figure 1, the relationship between debt and growth and the threshold vary depending on the

country-specific sovereign risk which illustrates the heterogeneity stated in some empirical

literatures. In a country with a high sovereign risk  (γ = 0.2), the relationship between public

debt and growth shows a humped-shaped pattern and the threshold is around 90% (See

Reinhart and Rogoff (2010)). Nevertheless, in a country that has extremely high sovereign

risk (γ = 0.9), it shows an inverted U-shaped curve, but the turning point is much lower, which

is around 40%-50%. Especially, when the debt level is higher than the sustainable level, even

a small change in debt-GDP ratio would cause a dramatic decrease of growth. The finding

demostrates the statement in  E gert (2012) saying that with the data from 13 OECD countries,

there is a strong negative nonlinear link between debt and growth and the turning point is

between 20% and 60%.  In the benchmark case, when the debt-GDP ratio exceeds a relatively

high debt threshold, there is a substantial reduction in growth.19 In this case, fiscal stimulus

could be effective to improve the economic growth. All above three senarios display the idea

that a certain level of debt has a positive effect on economic growth, but beyond that level

where it would be sustainable, debt may drag the economic growth.

With a sovereign risk, a debt reduction could reduce the sovereign interest rate and make the

inflation expectations lower. Also, the tax rate declines at the same time following the

assumption on tax rule. Both increase the market value of wealth held by the private sector

debt means lower government revenue. The government spending should fall and this effect

may be amplified by fiscal multiplier.

Under goods market clearing condition, output consists of aggregate demand, exports and

government spending. From equation (23), in a fixed exchange rate regime, lower CPI

inflation expectation indicates a higher real exchange rate, which has a positive impact on

imports and a negative impact on exports. If the price elasticity of the demand of imports and

the price elasticity of the demand of exports are small, both the variation in exports and the

variation in import are small. That means, under this assumption, the increase in aggregate

demand is essentially triggered by the increase in the demand of domestic goods.

Based on the arguments above, both the shape and the threshold in describing the relationship

between debt and growth, depend on the comparison of wealth effect and fiscal multiplier

effect. With a small debt reduction, a higher sovereign risk results in a more significant

change in sovereign interest rate which leads to a larger effect on the aggregate demand.

When the wealth effect dominates the fiscal multiplier effect, it shows a negative relationship.

When the fiscal multiplier effect dominates, a positive relationship is presented.

## 4. Conclusion

This paper establishes a DSGE model in a small open economy with sovereign risk to argue

the particularly heated debate about the relationship between debt and growth. The model

tries to mimic a small open economy in the real world, on an extreme but feasible assumption

that the domestic government bonds interest rate and the foreign bonds interest rate are

identical. The risk premium reflects that home country is risky and it is introduced through a

debt-elastic interest rate. I introduce a country-specific sovereign risk parameter into the debt-

elastic interest rate rule to find a country-specific relationship between debt and growth. A

general relationship between debt and growth may not work in a particular country. The

relationship should depend on the country-specific parameter. Moreover, I assume the small

open economy follows a fixed exchange rate rule, which indicates that fiscal policy should be

implemented to stabilize the economy in the medium and the short run. I include an artificial

Taylor rule, the only role of which is to provide a signal about the interest rate smoothing that

responds to economic fluctuations gradually.


<!-- Page 22 -->


20

My paper finds some evidence of the relationship between debt and growth from a theoretical

perspective. The two most important contributions of this paper are that it is the first to

investigate the relationship between debt and growth within a DSGE framework and also the

model can illustrate some typical empirical results. The relationship between public debt and

growth shows a huge difference with different country-specific sovereign risk parameters.

Three scenarios are considered. With a higher sovereign risk, a small change in debt-GDP

ratio indicates a bigger variation in sovereign interest rate, which leads to a lower confidence

of the home country and thus a lower level of investment. In a country with a high sovereign

risk, it shows an inverted U-shaped relation with a threshold around 90%. With an extremely

high sovereign risk, the relationship is still inverse U-shaped, but with a rather low threshold.

In the benchmark case, when the debt-GDP ratio exceeds a relatively high debt threshold,

there is a substantial reduction in growth, that is, fiscal stimulus could be effective to improve

economic growth in such countries where sovereign risk is not that high.

What level of debt-GDP ratio the government should keep if the government would like to

maximize its economic growth? Should the priority be fiscal stimulus to increase growth or

fiscal austerity to reduce debt? The strategies government should implement to improve its

growth depend on the country-specific sovereign risk. Fiscal stimulus could be effective to

improve the economic growth since in some countries sovereign risk is not that high.

Incorporating banking sector seems to be an interesting extension. Other extensions, like tax

reforms, pension system reform, political distortion, are also fascinating directions.
